data.title: 5-year plan to boost livelihoods, concrete measures in policy address: John Lee
data.description:
Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to improve residents’ livelihoods through long-term strategies in the city’s first five-year plan, with concrete measures to be set out in the coming policy address.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Sunday that the administration would continue to uphold its people-oriented governance philosophy, focus on residents’ needs and push Hong Kong forward.
Lee will unveil Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and deliver the annual policy address on September 16. Lee said the arrangement would help the public understand how the two documents complemented each other.
“Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will enhance residents’ livelihoods and well-being through long-term development strategies. Meanwhile, the policy address will annually roll out concrete improvement measures on housing, livelihoods, medical care and other areas,” he said in a Facebook video.
Lee added that the government had consulted the public on the two documents over the past two months.
“We will consolidate views and incorporate them into our planning and policies to promote sustainable economic development, improve livelihoods, and join hands to create new opportunities in Hong Kong,” he said.

The video on Lee’s social media page also featured interviews with residents, who shared how various government initiatives had helped their families.
A subdivided flat tenant, surnamed Ng, who has used services at a community living room project, said the centre had helped her son, who has special education needs, improve his language skills and boost his confidence.
According to the video, since the scheme launched in 2023, the city’s 16 community living rooms have served about 9,000 subdivided flat households and recorded close to 2.2 million visits.
A working parent surnamed Cheung said the government’s School-based After-school Care Service Scheme had helped his daughter revise and take part in different extracurricular activities over the summer.
The scheme was expanded after the government lifted the service quota cap in the 2025 policy address. In the 2025-26 academic year, schools taking part offered more than 10,000 places to families.
A representative of ethnic minority care teams said members would proactively reach out to such families to share the latest government information and understand their needs.
The video noted that the city had 12 ethnic minority care teams. They had contacted about 18,000 ethnic minority households and conducted around 10,000 family visits.
Another resident shared how she had developed a habit of regular exercise and managed her high blood pressure through health initiatives.
More than 260,000 residents have taken part in the Chronic Disease Co-care Scheme, which provides convenient screening services for eligible residents.




Sze Lai-shan, deputy director of the Society for Community Organisation, said the coming policy address and five-year plan should prioritise poverty alleviation and protect employment opportunities for low-income residents.
“The government focuses on rewarding those who are unemployed and subsequently find a job. It should also explore ways to help jobseekers,” she said.
Sze suggested subsidising jobseekers and relaxing the asset limits for social security recipients to encourage the underprivileged to save.
She also urged the government to continue expanding existing social services, such as widening the network and extending the operating hours of the School-based After-school Care Service Scheme to enable more parents to take up employment.
Sze added that the administration could expand the community living room network by opening communal centres or schools, while care teams should focus on identifying high-risk households, such as low-income seniors with serious illnesses and people recovering from mental illness.
On Saturday, Lee said the two documents would promote steady economic development, attract more global firms to the Hong Kong park of a cross-border innovation and technology hub, and build the city into an international tertiary education hub.

data.title: Hong Kong open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease: labour chief
data.description:
Hong Kong labour authorities are open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease, the city’s labour chief has said, acknowledging the revamped heat warning system would have triggered stronger alerts on two exceptionally hot days last month.
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-shum said retrospective modelling showed the revised system would have issued a black warning on August 8 and a red alert on August 9, when the Observatory recorded 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) at its headquarters – the highest temperature since records began in 1884.
“If we applied the revamped Heat Stress at Work Warning system, we would have issued a red warning on August 9 and even a black warning on August 8,” Hui told a television programme on Sunday.
The heat stress warning system has three levels – amber, red and black – and advises employers on rest arrangements for outdoor workers or those in indoor environments without air conditioning.
Under the previous mechanism, only an amber warning was issued on August 9, prompting criticism from lawmakers, unions and meteorologists that the system failed to reflect the severity of the heat faced by outdoor workers.
Amber signals significant heat stress and advises employers to arrange additional rest periods, while black is the highest warning level, under which workers performing heavy or very heavy labour should suspend work.
The department subsequently revised the mechanism on August 28 by adding two triggers intended to make it more sensitive to extreme temperatures and strong solar radiation.
Hui said authorities would continue studying the performance of the revamped system and consider whether further adjustments were needed before the next hot season.
The labour chief also said the department was open to adding heatstroke to the city’s list of prescribed occupational diseases, a move long demanded by unions seeking to make it easier for affected workers to claim compensation.
“We have an open attitude towards the proposal, but there is work that needs to be done in between,” he said.
“We have not reached a conclusion, but we believe this is an area worth studying.”

Hui said heatstroke and heat exhaustion suffered during employment could already qualify for compensation as work injuries under existing legislation.
But he acknowledged workers could face difficulties proving that their condition was caused by their job rather than underlying health problems, as classifying an illness as occupational requires an established medical link with a particular working environment or pattern.
The department was exploring whether medical and pathological information from confirmed work-related heatstroke cases could be compiled as a reference database for healthcare professionals assessing future claims, he added.
“If these methods can make the process faster and improve its accuracy, I think they may help workers in need,” Hui said, adding that there was no timetable for the proposal.
Hui stressed that the issuance of a higher heat stress warning did not automatically require an entire construction site to suspend operations.
Employers could maintain work by conducting risk assessments in advance and adopting measures such as providing cooling stations, ventilated clothing, fans, shade and rescheduling physically demanding work away from the hottest hours, he said.
The department previously estimated that the revised mechanism could produce red warnings on four to seven days annually and black alerts on one or two days.

data.title: Fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than double in first half of 2026
data.description:
Fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with a year earlier, with nine deaths recorded, as police point to cyclists ignoring traffic signals and road signs.
Overall, there were 59 fatal traffic accidents in the first six months of the year, killing 63 people, up more than 40 per cent from a year earlier. Fatal cases involving bicycles surged 125 per cent, accounting for nine of those deaths.
“Most cyclists tend to ignore traffic signals and road signs, and ride without carefully observing surrounding road conditions,” a police spokesman said.
“Combined with dangerous behaviours such as riding on the pavement, illegally carrying passengers and riding side by side, this largely increases the risk of accidents.”
In response, the New Territories North police region launched a cycling safety campaign on August 1, combining street promotions, community lectures, interactive games and social media outreach to target high-risk behaviours and raise awareness of related laws and road safety.
Officers then carried out a targeted enforcement operation on September 4 and 5, after the education phase, issuing nine warnings and 159 summonses over the two days.
“Bicycles have become a common mode of transport for many residents, but some riders showed weak awareness of road safety, with various offences risking serious accidents at any time,” the spokesman said.
Police said they would continue the two-pronged strategy of education and enforcement, urging cyclists to strictly follow the Road Traffic Ordinance, stay alert to signals and road conditions, switch on front white and rear red lights at night, and avoid running red lights or riding against traffic.

data.title: Calls for Hong Kong anti-stalking law after man acquitted of following teen girl
data.description:
Lawmakers and a government adviser have called for anti-stalking legislation to close a loophole that makes prosecuting repeated harassment difficult in Hong Kong, following the acquittal of a man who followed a teenage girl to her secondary school classroom.
Some experts said the government should revisit a proposal for such legislation raised 26 years ago, after the magistrate who acquitted the defendant of a loitering charge also noted the absence of laws to criminalise stalking under certain circumstances.
Unlike many jurisdictions with dedicated legislation to protect victims, Hong Kong can only prosecute suspects under a patchwork of different laws, with even the statutes on doxxing viewed as insufficient to punish cyberstalking.
The 57-year-old government statistician was found not guilty on August 25 of following the 16-year-old girl to her school and loitering outside the classroom in July last year.
The man also allegedly followed her during her commute to school for two to three years. He told police the girl resembled an old friend and he wanted to know her.
Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong said that loitering causing concern was inappropriate for addressing the defendant’s actions, which could not be handled under existing criminal laws.
Lam also noted that the Law Reform Commission had suggested introducing legislation targeting stalking in the past.
The commission raised the suggestion in 2000, but the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau put it on hold in 2014 after concluding that there were “no favourable conditions for us to pursue the matter further”.
Ronny Tong Ka-wah, a barrister and a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, suggested launching a new public consultation on the legislation.
“The government back then shelved the proposal because it said society had not reached a consensus on this law … But presently, I honestly see no reason to object,” he noted.
Tong added that although it was possible to pursue civil action against a stalker, the threshold for an injunction application was high. Typically, ordinary people will be unable to afford the lengthy proceedings.
Dedicated legislation would better protect the public, he said.

Lawmaker Alex Fan Hoi-kit, a barrister by profession, said the government should review the commission’s suggestion again and take into account changes in Hong Kong law over the years.
Doxxing that exposed a person’s personal information online became prosecutable under the Personal Data (Privacy) (Amendment) Ordinance enacted in 2021.
Fan said the acquittal should prompt authorities to reconsider whether to go a step further regarding criminal liability for stalking.
Legal sector lawmaker Nick Chan Hiu-fung raised doubts over whether the privacy laws could address cyberstalking, which took many forms.
“Privacy legislation cannot serve as a surrogate for anti-stalking laws,” the lawyer said.
Chan said that consultation with different stakeholders took time, but he stressed the proposal should be examined again.
However, veteran criminal lawyer Stephen Hung Wan-shun said enacting proposed legislation that had been shelved so long ago would be highly unlikely.
Hung, a commission member, said the existing loitering law might be enough to cover offences in various scenarios, as the key to securing a conviction was proving suspects were in a place where they should not have been.
But Hung noted that the defendant in the latest case was present at the school during its open day, which made his appearance legitimate in a way.
“If one wants to resurrect the commission’s proposal, there must be something significant to have happened,” he said.
“It has been shelved for many years; it would be difficult for the government to bring it up for discussion.”

data.title: In Focus|Will geopolitics put a potential Musk merger between a rocket and a hard place?
data.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.
The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.
In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.
While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.
That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.
Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.
“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”
The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.
Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another
Seth Goldstein, Morningstar
Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.
While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.
“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.
The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.
Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.
The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.
“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.
Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.


Can Tesla do without China?
At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.
Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.
Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.
Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.
Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.
China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.




“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.
“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”
Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.
Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.
Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.
Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.
And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.
The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised
Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney
Between Washington and Beijing
Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.
Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.
Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.
The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.
But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.
Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.
How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.
“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”
She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”


Tesla lays the first bricks
Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.
It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.
Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.
CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.
Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.
“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.
Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.
SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.




Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.
However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.
While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.
Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’
However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.
“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”
Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.
A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.
Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.


“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.
Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.
Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.
These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.
Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.
“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.
Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.
“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

data.title: China’s AI ‘little giant’ Yunxi Technology files for Hong Kong IPO: sources
data.description:
Yunxi Technology, officially one of China’s “little giants”, has submitted a confidential initial public offering application to Hong Kong’s stock exchange, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Guangzhou-based start-up was valued at 10 billion yuan (US$1.27 billion) in its latest private funding round and was working with Bocom International on the deal, aiming to raise “several hundred million [US] dollars”, said the people, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue.
While the listing is targeted to take place by the end of this year, the timing and size remain subject to change, the people said. High-profile backers include Chinese billionaire Jack Ma’s Yunfeng Capital and investment firm HSG Capital.
Yunxi did not immediately respond to South China Morning Post’s request for comment.
Founded in 2016, Yunxi provides end-to-end digital growth products and tools to help major clients across the consumer goods, retail, real estate and automotive sectors integrate artificial intelligence into their operations.
The company is one of China’s nationally recognised “little giants”, a label awarded by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to specialised, innovative small- and medium-sized enterprises that focus on niche markets, master core technologies and hold high market shares.
By November 2025, China had nurtured over 17,600 such firms, with plans to expand that total to 22,000 by 2030, according to a recent ministry notice.
According to a source familiar with the transaction, Yunxi had applied to list under Chapter 18C of the Hong Kong stock exchange rules – a specialised framework designed for high-growth firms in advanced technology sectors.
Official data from the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing showed that by the end of March, 14 companies had gone public under this specific chapter, raising a combined HK$28.4 billion (US$3.62 billion), with additional applications under review.

data.title: Elderly hiker airlifted to hospital after collapsing at scenic spot in Hong Kong
data.description:
An elderly man has been airlifted to hospital after collapsing while hiking at a popular scenic spot in southern Hong Kong.
Police said they received a report at 9.13am on Sunday from a passer-by about an incident involving a man in his seventies at Yuk Kwai Shan on Ap Lei Chau
An ambulance was dispatched to the scene, while a Government Flying Service helicopter took him to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan.
Yuk Kwai Shan, also known as Mount Johnston, is a scenic spot popular for its sea views but is considered a dangerous destination because of its steepness and lack of established hiking trails or shade from the sun.
Police had previously cautioned residents against hiking at the spot.
In April, three hikers lost their way on the hill when a rainstorm warning signal was in effect and were eventually rescued by firefighters.
In August last year, three hikers were taken to hospital on the same day after suffering bee attacks on Yuk Kwai Shan.

data.title: Hong Kong’s billionaires, Treasury yields hit 4.78%: the numbers moving marketsChina’s expanding outbound capital and US bonds’ surging yields are in spotlight this week.
data.description:
China has been expanding its outbound-investment channels, with a new quota granted and greater overseas allocation by the nation’s pension fund. However, the financial world beyond the mainland is seeing volatility as US bond yields hit 20-month highs.
Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week.
US$6.84 billion in new quotas for mutual funds
China’s foreign-exchange regulator approved US$6.84 billion in new, qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) quotas for mutual funds, insurers and banks’ wealth-management units by the end of August, according to data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, expanding their capacity to invest in overseas assets.
Eighteen money managers, including China Asset Management and GF Fund Management, received US$100 million each, while more than 20 Chinese banks’ wealth-management units received quotas for the first time.
Hong Kong has 106 billionaires, second only to New York
Hong Kong remained the world’s second-largest billionaire hub with 106 billionaires, trailing only New York, which had 164, according to wealth data provider Altrata.
Beijing and Shenzhen also ranked among the world’s 15 cities with the most billionaires, helped by wealth creation from the AI boom.
US 10-year Treasury yield hits 20-month high
The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.78 per cent on Tuesday, its highest level in 20 months, as investors sold government debt amid concerns over the country’s fiscal outlook.
The move came as US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told G20 finance ministers that Washington was a leader in tackling sovereign debt problems in emerging markets, even as rising borrowing costs in the US highlighted the challenges facing the country. Benchmark yields in Japan and the UK have also climbed to multi-decade highs.
China’s national pension offshore assets hit record US$86 billion
China’s National Social Security Fund more than doubled its offshore investments in three years to a record 580.02 billion yuan (US$86 billion) at the end of 2025, as it sought higher returns through greater exposure to overseas markets.
Offshore assets accounted for 15.23 per cent of the fund’s total assets, the highest proportion on record, according to its annual report released on Tuesday.

data.title: Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
data.description:
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.
It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.
“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.
“If I have to do a massive round of work just to sail for one or two days, I might as well sail in Hong Kong.”
He added that he would rather take a commercial ferry to Dongao for a holiday.
Still, the 66-year-old veteran mariner gave the voyage a score of 60 out of 100 and viewed it as a worthwhile test run.
Yu was among 139 participants aboard 16 yachts from Hong Kong and Macau that sailed to Dongao under the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme. Launched in June, the scheme allows eligible Hong Kong and Macau vessels to enter designated Guangdong waters for tourism.
The voyage, which took place over the weekend, was the scheme’s largest cross-border flotilla to date. It gave visitors a taste of the island’s seafood, hotel suites and natural scenery.
An eventful voyage
Early on August 29, the flotilla left the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in Causeway Bay for Dongao, about 36 nautical miles (53.7km) southwest of the city.
The journey took between 6½ and 8½ hours, depending on the yacht’s speed.
For participants such as 60-year-old financial executive Noel Chan and his 16-year-old son Nigel, it was family time. Chan sailed his 45-foot cruiser, Rampage, in 15-knot winds, while the pair chatted and shared drinks on deck.
“The wind speed was very good, conditions were great,” Nigel Chan said.

Mabel Tsim, an IT professional and sailor, described the eight-hour journey as a stress-relieving bonding experience.
She compared Dongao Island’s idyllic setting and sea views with those of a Southeast Asian resort in Thailand or Bali, Indonesia.
“For us as crew members, we focus on the journey itself,” she said. “The destination is a place for leisure, but more importantly, the process is sailing … For city dwellers, it is very stress-relieving.”
But hardware limitations soon became apparent. Immigration procedures at the designated port on Guishan Island took about 20 minutes – visitors entered a building, went upstairs for home return permit and baggage checks, then waited downstairs while officers checked vessel documents.
However, there was only one yacht berth, meaning vessels had to circle at sea for about 15 minutes while waiting for the previous yacht to clear.
One yacht suffered an incident at the port when its propeller broke off and sank to the seabed.
After navigating intermittent rain, the fleet arrived at Dongao, an island heavily reliant on mainland families visiting at weekends. But its temporary pontoons proved inadequate, with one yacht running aground twice in shallow water.


In the end, 13 of the 16 yachts stayed on the island for one night, while the rest remained for two.
Before setting sail, a yacht typically had to spend thousands of Hong Kong dollars to meet government requirements, including a US$1,500 vessel inspection and 3,000 yuan (US$447) in clearance fees, excluding hotel, food and other expenses.
For some participants, the time and expense were still worthwhile.
“I think out of 100 marks, I would say 85 to 90, so no such complaint … [the mainland is] really, really helpful for this [scheme] … [they] didn’t give you any hassle,” Noel Chan said.
His son Nigel compared the cost of sailing to Zhuhai with a friend’s experience in the United Kingdom.
“It’s 100 per cent more affordable, and it’s a much more pleasant experience,” he said.
While committed sailors and industry advocates regard the scheme’s early problems as necessary growing pains on the path to a world-class Greater Bay Area maritime economy, more pragmatic yacht owners remain divided over whether sailing north is worth the effort.
The yacht economy
For those with a team to navigate the administrative hurdles, the value proposition can be striking. Noel Chan said he spent just several thousand yuan on Marriott sea-view suites and other expenses for his group of 12.
He said the trip cost a fraction of a comparable stay in Hong Kong, and voiced concern that it could lead to a further outflow of Hong Kong consumer spending to the mainland.
“You go to Hong Kong, have a bad dinner, you spend that money already. So I think it’s a big challenge [for the] Hong Kong economy,” he said. “The money moved here again by sea instead of Hong Kong cars going [through the northbound vehicle scheme].”
The flotilla was a boon for some hotels.
A representative from the island’s five-star Gree Dongao Hotel said that the flotilla booked nearly 70 rooms, filling the 268-room property on August 29.

The hotel is part of the state-owned Zhuhai Gree Group, which has invested about 4 billion yuan since 2009 to develop a high-end hotel cluster on Dongao. The cluster also includes a 257-room Marriott and the cliffside Alila resort, which has 103 suites and is already attracting Hong Kong yachting people.
Dongfa Seafood Restaurant co-owner Zhou Shunfang, 60, marvelled at the flotilla but said she had not seen an influx of high-spending yacht guests. She suspected touts had intercepted them at the pier before they discovered her long-established restaurant.
Charting a smoother course
Liao Kai, president of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said about 50 yachts had obtained temporary nationality certificates, allowing them to use the scheme to travel to the Greater Bay Area.
Participants broadly agreed that the cross-border experience would require major upgrades to both its policy framework and physical infrastructure before it could unlock the full economic potential of Greater Bay Area waters.
At the policy level, reducing the barriers to entry is crucial. The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club had called for cross-border costs to be harmonised, vice-commodore Joseph Chu said. He suggested that northbound fees should be cut from thousands of Hong Kong dollars to match the nominal HK$58 charged for southbound vessels.

He argued that equalising the fees would turn special expeditions into more frequent trips, similar to Hong Kong residents travelling to Shenzhen for afternoon tea before returning home.
Yu echoed the call for less bureaucracy. He urged authorities across the border to drop the allegedly redundant “temporary nationality certificate” and accept surveys carried out by Hong Kong-approved professionals, rather than requiring separate and costly mainland inspections.
Workarounds to reduce costs are also emerging. Liao said traditional commercial shipping agencies had charged tens of thousands of dollars for customs clearance, prompting the Zhuhai Yacht Association to set up a dedicated agency to deal with paperwork. The move helped reduce outbound clearance fees to around 3,000 yuan for the flotilla.

On the water, relatively simple logistical changes could reduce delays. Noel Chan recommended staggered arrival times for yachts at clearance ports such as Guishan, to prevent bottlenecks that leave vessels circling offshore.
Tsim said authorities should find a way to process several boats at once. She also called for less rigid point-to-point travel rules, allowing yachts to visit more than one destination on the same itinerary.
Infrastructure remains a major constraint. Both Yu and Noel Chan said robust floating moorings, and more of them, were urgently needed at destinations such as Dongao Island to stop yachts having to “double park” in unsafe conditions.
Gao Jun, an associate professor at Sun Yat-sen University’s school of tourism management, said Zhuhai needed to improve tourist spending opportunities and amenities to extend the value chain beyond its 20-year manufacturing base in Pingsha.
By taking advantage of new self-navigating repair policies in Jinwan, cross-border access points and related services, Zhuhai aims to capture longer-term value from yacht maintenance and berthing, rather than relying solely on weekend tourism.
Liao said four yachts had successfully sailed to Jinwan, undergone major repairs and returned to Hong Kong since the self-navigating vessel repair policy was launched in March.
He added that more than 20 other vessels were applying to use the service.
Industry leaders urged patience. Chu compared the scheme’s early administrative and infrastructure problems with the chaotic early days of Hong Kong International Airport before it developed into a global aviation hub.
Stakeholders are now preparing for the anticipated launch of southbound travel.
Liao said he had heard from local authorities that the southbound scheme might open in September.

data.title: From ‘slop’ to prime time: how AI dramas are shaking up China’s TV industry
data.description:
From low-quality “slop” such as soap operas starring humanlike cats and dating shows featuring anthropomorphic fruit, to increasingly slick productions realistic enough to pass for live action, artificial intelligence-generated video dramas have become almost inescapable on Chinese social media feeds.
This week, the format graduated to prime time. A fully AI-generated adaptation of the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West debuted on Hunan Satellite Television, a major state-owned broadcaster known for its hit entertainment programming and its streaming platform Mango TV.
The 30-episode series, with each instalment running about 40 minutes, went from commission to broadcast in just three months. Production is still ongoing – the director told local media that later episodes would be continuously refined based on audience feedback.
The premiere delivered a sharp jolt to China’s long-depressed media and entertainment sector. Shares in Mango Excellent Media, the listed unit of the Hunan broadcaster, hit their 20 per cent daily trading limit twice this week before paring gains. The surge added more than 13 billion yuan (US$1.9 billion) to its market value, signalling a strong return of investor enthusiasm.
“This sends a clear signal of policy support,” said Guo Guo, a Beijing-based producer at a leading film and television company. “AI drama is going mainstream.”
The technology has hit the accelerator across the content industry.
Guo, who began working on AI-generated content (AIGC) projects this year, said a 10-person team could turn out a 100-minute vertical drama in a week, while a more sophisticated long-form production could move at the rate of one 45-minute episode a week.
Viewers can be surprisingly immune to the glitches
Liu Zhanhao, producer
According to the China Netcasting Services Association, 367,000 microdramas were released across Chinese platforms in the first half of this year. More than 74 per cent were AI-generated – an average of more than 1,500 new AI dramas a day.
Production teams are rapidly adapting to the new landscape.
On a fully AI-generated project, many fixtures of a conventional set – art departments, set crews, cinematographers, lighting technicians and actors – were no longer required, bringing costs down “exponentially”, said Liu Zhanhao, a producer who also moved into AI content this year.
In their place is a new kind of worker known in the industry as a “card puller”: part prompt engineer, part visual editor. They feed reference images and prompts into a model, then repeatedly adjust the inputs until it produces a usable shot.
Liu’s latest project, a 120-minute science-fiction mystery billed as a premium AI drama, is scheduled to appear on Mango TV this autumn.
“The large model developers are the newest claimants on the profits of the film and television industry,” Liu said.
His team iterated with the technology quickly, shifting from ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 to Seedance 2.5 in July once it was available, and spent most of the budget on generation.


Video generators are still far from perfect. Maintaining consistency of characters and settings, interpreting complex texts and overcoming limits on clip length remained bottlenecks, Liu said.
Guo had the same view, saying the models still struggled in scenes with especially high “emotional density”.
Platforms are nevertheless urging producers to make more. Streaming services including Mango TV, iQiyi, Tencent Video, and Douyin and ByteDance’s dedicated short-drama platform Hongguo are offering cash subsidies and algorithmic traffic boosts for AIGC productions.
Volume has arrived faster than quality.
“Viewers can be surprisingly immune to the glitches,” Liu said. “They’re watching what we call ‘brain-off’ gratification dramas. They want the twists, the melodrama, the exaggeration. They’re chasing a feeling.”
Ivy Yang, founder of Wavelet Strategy, a consultancy, believed short drama was the format most likely to devolve into cookie-cutter AI slop.
“Even before AI, the production logic was to cater to templates that algorithms rewarded – the domineering CEO, the revenge arc, humiliation followed by a comeback, time travel – at the lowest possible cost, highest speed and strongest possible dopamine hit,” Yang said.
She added that AI has pushed the cost of replicating those formulas towards zero.
“The immediate effect [of consuming this kind of content] is a systematic rise in tolerance for low-quality content,” she said.
Yang also worried most about younger viewers, who were still developing their narrative and aesthetic judgment. What was being eroded was “patience – for ambiguity, for set-up, for anything that asked the viewer to do some of the thinking”, she said.
Producer Liu said he expected inferior productions to be eliminated quickly as competition intensified, much as China’s once-ubiquitous copycat mobile phones eventually disappeared.
China’s cyberspace watchdog this week said it scrubbed millions of pieces of AI content – fake news, explicit and violent material, impersonation and safety violations involving minors – in a sweeping campaign against abuse of generative technology.
“The film and television industry is anxious about AI,” said Bryce Gu, who still produces live-action series. Distributors now asked for AI involvement in almost every project, he said, including some for which the technology was plainly ill-suited.
“The industry has always been protected by formidable barriers to entry, and AI has largely lowered them,” Gu said. “It can help a talented person get noticed much faster. But it cannot supply the talent.”

data.title: AI boom is hiding cracks in US markets, Nomura warnsBank flags US risk premium as AI surge falters, undermining ‘Tina’ or ‘there is no alternative’ to dollar assets.
data.description:
The artificial intelligence boom has signalled growing risks in the US economy and capital markets, with a setback in the technology rally potentially triggering a sharp correction in US assets and weakening the dollar, according to a Nomura report.
“The AI boom has masked a rising US risk premium,” Nomura analysts led by Rob Subbaraman said in a report on Thursday, warning that the concentration of global savings in US dollar assets had left investors increasingly exposed to a reversal in the AI-driven US equity rally.
The ratio of US net international investment position (NIIP) liabilities to the combined assets of all net creditor nations has risen to 80 per cent, according to the Japanese investment bank.
US NIIP liabilities reached US$21.9 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 71 per cent of gross domestic product, while the country’s portfolio liabilities have quadrupled to US$37.4 trillion in March 2026 from US$9.2 trillion before the global financial crisis, the bank’s data showed.
“We attempt to debunk the assumed robustness of ‘Tina’,” the bank said, referring to the belief that “there is no alternative” to US assets.
The growing exposure meant a sharp decline in US equities could have broader implications for global capital flows, particularly if foreign investors began to reduce their holdings of US assets, according to Nomura.
Despite the strong profit growth of US equities supported by the AI boom, the bank flagged high valuations, uncertain adoption, competition from cheaper Chinese large language models (LLMs) and constraints on computing power, memory and electricity.
A setback in AI could expose vulnerabilities masked by the equity rally and trigger a broader risk-off move, according to the bank.
Foreign investors’ large exposure to US portfolio assets, together with leverage and circular financing linked to the AI investment boom, could amplify the impact, it added.
Nomura estimated that US portfolio assets would need to fall by more than 30 per cent – comparable to a global financial crisis-scale repatriation – to fully offset the decline in US portfolio liabilities.

data.title: Signalling fault disrupts Hong Kong high-speed rail service, delaying 15 trains
data.description:
At least 15 high-speed cross-border train services were delayed after a signalling fault prompted a 45-minute disruption of northbound services in Hong Kong on Sunday morning.
The Transport Department said at around 8.30am that the MTR Corporation had notified authorities that high-speed rail services would be delayed due to a “signal fault”.
At around 9.15am, the department said the MTR had resolved the signal issues, and high-speed rail services were gradually resuming normally.
It said passengers could check the official 12306 train service app and the relevant MTR website for details.
According to 12306, at least 15 northbound trains were delayed, including those to Futian, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Fuzhou, Zhangjiajie, Xian, Tianjin and Chengdu.
Some passengers took to Chinese social media platform RedNote to voice their frustration over the disruption.
“I don’t know what happened in West Kowloon Station from about 7am to 8.30am, but all trains were stuck and weren’t allowed into the station,” a RedNote user wrote. “I waited on the train for about one hour before I could finally get off.”
Another user posted that his train was scheduled for 9.40am, but was delayed by about 20 minutes while he was travelling to Shenzhen to shop.

data.title: Why Chelsea football shirts are making Hong Kong fans nervous about crypto laws
data.description:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.
Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.
Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.
Only two stablecoin issuers are currently licensed in Hong Kong – Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC.
Ahead of the enactment of the Stablecoins Ordinance on August 1, 2025, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned on its website that “it will be illegal for any person to … actively market the issue of unlicensed [fiat-referenced stablecoins] to the public”.
Winnie Choi, a Chelsea fan of 12 years, was among those worried about breaking the law.
“After looking up the law, I still do not understand whether it is a problem to wear the jersey,” she said.
Choi suggested that the HKMA issue a clear, “down-to-earth” guideline on whether wearing the shirt with the USDC logo constituted promotion.
Danny*, a club supporter for more than 20 years, said ordinary football fans would not have the awareness to identify if the shirt promoted an unregulated stablecoin.
“If I wear it, who will enforce the law? Will I be arrested by police?” he said.
Danny said he would not buy the new jersey until authorities clarified whether it was legal to wear it.

Hammer Chung, owner of football apparel shop DirectSoccer in Mong Kok, said he was unsure whether it was legal to sell replica jerseys with the USDC logo.
He added that he hoped regulators would clarify the matter.
But Chung noted that many of the kits for other football clubs that he sold also bore the logos of illegal gambling websites.
“Are we also promoting for them by selling the shirts?” he said.
The HKMA said it would not comment on individual cases, but noted the ordinance prohibited the “active marketing” or advertising of unauthorised stablecoin activity in Hong Kong.
Whether an act constituted actively marketing to the public was determined on a case-by-case basis, a spokesman said.
Factors considered by the HKMA included the languages used in the marketing messages, whether they targeted people living in the city, whether a Hong Kong domain name was used and whether a detailed marketing plan was in place to promote the activity.
A specific exemption was provided to publishers and live broadcasters who merely published content created by others, as long as they satisfied the relevant conditions set out in the provision and considered the relevant facts and circumstances, he said.

Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung expressed concerns that fans donning the new Chelsea shirt in public could be “problematic”, as it all depended on how the HKMA defined active marketing.
“There are so many grey areas,” he said, adding that he dared not wear T-shirts sporting the logos of unlicensed crypto trading platforms after the licensing regime was put in place by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).
Li said USDC was the second-largest stablecoin in the world, and it was ridiculous that it was labelled as “unlicensed” under local legislation.
He also said it was difficult to regulate the promotion of cryptocurrencies within a certain jurisdiction in the age of the internet because they were issued globally. “How can you say something legal in other countries is illegal here?”
The ordinance provides an exemption for promoting unlicensed stablecoins across various media and digital platforms, including live broadcasts, provided the person did not devise and exercised no control over the content of the advertisement.
“A group of players on TV is wearing [shirts with] this logo … it’s impossible that it isn’t an advertisement. We’re looking at them the entire game, right?” Li said.


Tanna Chong, head of public policy at VerifyVASP, a digital assets compliance company, called for enhanced consumer protection through disclaimers before every match, similar to warning messages in moneylending advertisements.
“They would be clear reminders that the programme contains these materials [about cryptocurrency], and that those companies actually do not have a licence in Hong Kong,” she said.
Chong, who helped draft the ordinance during her time in government, said there was no hard and fast rule to define active marketing, noting that it was a concept determined on a case-by-case basis considering various contextual factors.
She said neither Circle nor Chelsea had control over the broadcasting of matches in Hong Kong, which involved a deal between NowTV and the Premier League, and had not actively implemented a marketing campaign in the city.
Circle was not “by way of business providing services” in the city either, she added.
She also reassured fans that there was no problem with wearing the Blues’ shirt with the USDC logo, as wearers were not the service provider.
“Unless [the wearer] is a Circle employee walking down the street in a Chelsea jersey. In that case, you need to establish that Circle instructed him to wear it with the intent of targeting a Hong Kong audience,” she said.
An HKT spokesman said Now TV strictly complied with all relevant Hong Kong laws and regulations.
The South China Morning Post has reached out to Circle and Chelsea FC for comment.
The West London club’s latest deal followed a collective agreement by all 20 Premier League clubs to phase out front-of-shirt gambling sponsors. But the Blues are not the first team to partner with the crypto sector.

OKX and Kraken, both virtual asset trading platforms unlicensed in Hong Kong, are the sleeve sponsors of Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur.
Chelsea itself also partnered with crypto platform BingX, which is also unlicensed in Hong Kong, for an official training kit front sponsorship.
During their visit to the city last month, Chelsea players wore the training kit with the BingX logo during an open training session at Kai Tak Stadium.
Players from City and Spurs also wore kits sporting the OKX and Kraken logos during their friendlies in Hong Kong in August this year and July last year, respectively.
Similar clauses regulating the promotion of unlicensed virtual asset trading platforms are present in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance.
The SFC said it would not comment on specific cases. It added that it would take into account all marketing and advertising activities in their totality in considering the appropriate course of action.
Kraken said that it maintained jurisdiction-specific controls designed to ensure its activities complied with applicable local laws.
The trading platform also stressed that its partnership with Tottenham Hotspur was a global brand sponsorship.
It did not reflect an offer, solicitation or promotion of Kraken’s virtual asset trading services in jurisdictions where those activities were restricted, it added.
The SCMP has reached out to Manchester City, OKX, Tottenham Hotspur and BingX for comment.
*Name changed at interviewee’s request.

data.title: Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying to give live lecture from space
data.description:
Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members will deliver a live lecture from space for students and teachers in the city and neighbouring Macau.
Hong Kong authorities revealed on Saturday plans for live broadcasts of “Tiangong Class” to take place soon, without specifying the date and time.
The activity, jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency, includes an expert lecture, an in-orbit demonstration and a question-and-answer session to showcase the environment in space.
Hong Kong’s Education Bureau will arrange for primary and secondary schoolteachers and students to watch the live broadcast on campuses on the day of the event, while a delegation from Macau will visit the city to attend “Tiangong Class”.
A live online broadcast will be arranged on the Information Services Department’s website and Facebook page, as well as local television stations.
“This will be a valuable aerospace science education activity, allowing students to watch live demonstrations of science experiments conducted in the unique environment of space, with a view to enhancing their knowledge of aerospace science and stimulating their interest in learning,” a spokesperson said.
“Students can also learn from the three astronauts of the Shenzhou-23 crew, who are currently carrying out a manned space mission on the Tiangong Space Station, thereby building their aspirations, encouraging them to be daring to explore, further cultivating their patriotism and strengthening national identity.”
The space mission featuring Lai launched in May. Lai, 43, was a police superintendent and a mother of three. She is serving as the payload specialist for the mission.
One crew member will remain in orbit for one year to study the long-term effects on astronaut health and to improve in-orbit medical support, while the other two, including Lai, will return in November.
