data.title: Robot guide dog debuts in China amid severe lack of the furry kind
data.description:
A Chinese defence industry research facility has unveiled what it calls the world’s first wheeled and legged robot guide dog for visually impaired people, in an example of the sector’s push into a growing range of civilian applications.
Hangzhou-based Zhiyuan Research Institute, affiliated with China North Industries Group, the country’s largest defence contractor, launched the robot, dubbed Xiaoyuan, on Friday at the China Care and Rehabilitation Expo in Beijing.
Equipped with wheels for smooth movement on flat ground and four legs for climbing stairs, the robot was designed to help visually impaired people navigate independently, according to the institute.
The wheeled design allowed the robot to move quietly, an important feature for those who rely on their hearing to perceive their surroundings, the institute said. Meanwhile, it could also identify overhead obstacles such as low-hanging branches, which could be difficult to detect with traditional mobility aids such as canes.
The robot offered centimetre-level outdoor positioning accuracy, with an error margin of less than 30 centimetres, while its obstacle-avoidance success rate was at least 99 per cent indoors and 96 per cent outdoors, according to the institute.
Xiaoyuan is connected to services including disability federation systems, an accessibility map and a remote assistance portal for volunteers, allowing users to seek help remotely when needed.
China has more than 17 million people with visual impairments, according to a report by state-run Xinhua News in May, citing the China Association of Persons with Visual Disabilities (CAPVD).
By comparison, the country has only around 400 guide dogs in service, according to CAPVD, which added that a guide dog costs around 200,000 yuan (US$29,776) and takes about a year to train.


The institute said it had reached strategic cooperation agreements with disability groups in the eastern province of Zhejiang, its capital Hangzhou and Inner Mongolia, and had begun pilot deployments and trials at locations including Hangzhou’s metro system and shopping centres.
Other developers are also working on expanding the application of robotics and AI in China.
For example, Beijing-based AI Robotics and Hangzhou-based RoboCT have developed exoskeleton robots used at hospitals and rehabilitation centres to help patients regain mobility.

data.title: How can future doctors blend clinical rigour with AI fluency and empathy?
data.description:
Medical experts have stressed that Hong Kong’s next generation of healthcare professionals must combine clinical rigour with emotional resilience, an open-minded approach to artificial intelligence (AI) and the drive to transform the sector.
The remarks came during a panel discussion on the first day of the inaugural Global Education Summit, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier.
“We always talk about people going north, going to Shenzhen … for medical services. But I would say that it’s a good thing for a future doctor. You’re going to be a doctor not just for 7 million people. You’re going to be a doctor for 18 million people,” Dr Chung Kin-lai, chief executive officer of CUHK Medical Centre, said on Saturday.
The discussion, titled “Powering Hong Kong’s healthcare talent pipeline: from medical education to research and industry impact”, explored how the sector was preparing young doctors and healthcare talent for this changing landscape.
The summit, which runs for two days, brought together about 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents from around the world to discuss regional talent development, AI integration and evolving academic pathways.
With AI reshaping clinical workflows, medical leaders warned that traditional metrics for evaluating future doctors were changing. Chung noted that soft skills had become increasingly vital.
“The old stuff when we ask about the ingredients to be a good doctor … are something like good language, good presentation, and also something like good memory,” Chung said.
“But nowadays, memory is not that important. When you ask the internet, when you ask AI, everything comes up.
“I think more important is your training of the other side – the soft side, your human touch.
“How you communicate with people, especially with empathy.”
Dr Kenneth Tsang, regional chief executive officer of IHH Healthcare North Asia and chief executive of Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong, highlighted a generational divide in technology adoption.
“What we found is that doctors in middle age and above are quite resilient when it comes to adopting AI. They actually resisted taking up AI,” he said.
“So we are now actually moving into finding the younger generation of doctors who are very open and already, I would say, very knowledgeable about AI to join us and work with us on AI and healthcare.”

With AI tools more prevalent, panellists told students that innovation required asking insightful questions, not just memorising answers.
Innovation also required asking insightful questions rather than just memorising answers, said Dr Ricky Chiu, chairman and chief executive officer of PHASE Scientific and adjunct associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, during the session curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm.
“My advice is really right now trying to learn how to ask the question that no one asks or ask the right question,” he said.
“If I ask AI what the best way to screen for cervical cancer is, AI will give me a textbook answer. There’s nothing useful about that, right? But if I ask AI, how come these tests are available but yet all the women are still not doing that? And you’ve got a company.”
Chiu encouraged students to view healthcare opportunities and career paths beyond traditional clinical roles, outlining three primary ways to contribute: treating patients; teaching doctors; and developing healthcare tools.
“A doctor saves lives one at a time, and I think it’s a great life’s work. A good diagnosis can really change people’s lives,” he said.
For students and parents considering medical studies, the experts also stressed that young people should ask themselves whether they understood it was a lifelong commitment before choosing this path.
Chung warned high-achieving students against choosing medicine out of habit or simply because it was a top priority, noting that the extensive training required could often take 12 to 15 years.
Tsang emphasised that real-world clinical readiness hinged on humility, while Chiu urged parents to let their children make their own choices, ensuring medicine was a genuine “lifetime dream”.
Echoing the transformation seen in medicine, an adjacent panel discussed the qualities that tech and innovation leaders looked for in the next generation of talent.
The panel featured industry leaders including Michael Yue, managing director and general manager of Google Hong Kong, Terry Wong, chief executive officer of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation, Winnie Ng, managing director and head of wealth and premier solutions, retail banking and wealth, Hong Kong, at HSBC, and Yiyin Zhao, managing director of Samsung Electronics Hong Kong.
Experts discussed some qualities they valued in future talent beyond academic results, including curiosity, adaptability, problem-solving and resilience.
They also stressed the importance of students maintaining “the attitude to keep learning” and the ability to build relationships, work with people, and have empathy for others.

data.title: Safety or hostility? Dog owners split over Hong Kong’s crackdown on leash rules
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities’ intensified enforcement against dog owners who fail to control their pets has drawn mixed reactions, with supporters welcoming improved safety and critics warning it is stoking panic and hostility.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department carried out inspections and enforcement operations across the city on Saturday following a spate of dog attacks in recent weeks.
Among those walking their pets at the West Kowloon Cultural District despite the heat were civil servant Mark Mak, 35, his wife and their two daughters.
Mak, who owns a six-year-old dog named Mori, said he always leashed his pet in public to prevent it from wandering or coming into contact with other dogs and disapproved of owners who did not.
“The inspections and enforcement are good for protecting the safety of people and pets. They should be continued as we don’t want to see any more tragedies,” he said.

Finance sector employee Kim Chan, also in his thirties, walked his nine-year-old black labradoodle, Charcoal, at the cultural district. Chan said that although his dog was well-behaved and non-aggressive, he always used a leash to protect it and avoid affecting others.
“The measures can improve protection and remind dog owners of their responsibilities as some people, including children, may be afraid of dogs,” he said.
But an owner of a 10-year-old mongrel, who gave only her surname, Cheung, said the stepped-up inspections had created panic in communities. She cited growing hostility from others, including taxi drivers refusing to give her and her dog a ride.
“Such measures only spread panic and make people think that having a dog is a problem,” Cheung, in her thirties, said.
Staff patrolled the cultural district with signs reminding people to leash their pets, a measure also observed at tech hub Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam, where some dog owners walked with their pets.
Retiree Betty Ngai, 63, and her husband were enjoying an outing with their four-year-old poodle at Cyberport.

Ngai said she kept her dog on a leash for most of the time outside despite its small size, and supported the government’s reinforced actions in response to recent attacks as a reminder to owners to keep pets under proper control.
Authorities stepped up enforcement against dog owners who fail to keep their pets under control during special operations over this weekend and on August 30.
The department said officers would step up inspections at public places where dogs congregated, and take immediate enforcement action without warning if keepers were found not to have properly controlled their dogs in accordance with legal requirements.
The department earlier said it conducted operations in Yuen Long, West Kowloon, Cyberport and Kai Tak on August 30, and would prosecute three dog owners for failing to keep large dogs on a leash in public areas.
Under the Rabies Ordinance, it is an offence to leave a dog unleashed in public areas or at any place from which it may wander into a public space. Offenders can be fined HK$10,000 (US$1,275) upon conviction.
Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, any dog weighing 20kg or more must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres. Anyone who fails to comply faces a maximum penalty of three months in prison and a HK$25,000 fine.
Last month, a 33-year-old pet training facility owner was mauled by a mixed-breed fighting dog registered as a mongrel. She was found dead nearby after the attack.
A 60kg mixed-breed dog killed a miniature poodle and a bichon frise in separate attacks near Yoho Mall in Yuen Long last month.

data.title: Machines now use AI more than humans, boosting cheap Chinese modelsAgentic AIs now use five times as many tokens as humans, giving lower-priced models from Chinese firms a competitive edge, analysts s
data.description:
The global artificial intelligence boom recently crossed a landmark threshold: autonomous agents now consume more than five times as much data as human users, triggering a surge in processing costs that is giving lower-priced Chinese models a competitive edge, according to analysts.
Unlike traditional chatbots that simply respond to human prompts, these agents operate independently to execute multi-step workflows, such as writing software, conducting research or managing business operations.
A single assignment can trigger a cascade of automated model calls as an agent plans its task, searches databases, invokes software tools and audits its own results.
This shift has dramatically altered the economics of AI deployment. Agentic requests consumed about 15 times more tokens – the basic units of data processed by an AI model – than standard human queries, according to data from model aggregator OpenRouter compiled by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
The data showed that daily token consumption from agentic workloads on OpenRouter hit 7.3 trillion in early August – 14 times the level six months earlier.
Agentic activity first surpassed human usage in February. By August, it accounted for over five times the 1.4 trillion tokens generated by human users on the platform.
Token usage will continue to grow exponentially as models become more capable and penetrate more scenarios
Sun Wenhao, TH Capital
Much of the increase came from cached prompt tokens – repeated portions of prompts, including system instructions, conversation histories and tool definitions, that can be reused without being fully processed again. Providers generally charge less for cached input because it requires less computation, although the rapid growth in overall volume could still increase corporate AI bills.
“Token usage will continue to grow exponentially as models become more capable and penetrate more scenarios,” said Sun Wenhao, a senior investment manager at Chinese deep tech venture investor TH Capital.
In China, daily token calls jumped 5,000-fold to 500 trillion in June this year from around 100 billion at the start of 2024, according to official data cited by state broadcaster CCTV.
To keep costs manageable, companies are increasingly turning to “model routing”, an approach where routine, repetitive tasks are directed to lower-cost models, reserving expensive, high-powered frontier models for complex reasoning, according to US enterprise software firm Salesforce.
“If everything runs on premium models, it is clearly too expensive,” Sun said, adding that coding and text-based research currently dominated agent usage, mostly assisting human workers rather than fully automating jobs.
Token demand could rise further once agents were trusted to carry out more tasks from beginning to end, he added.
The cost sensitivity could work to the advantage of Chinese open-weight models – AI systems that are released freely over the internet, allowing users with the necessary hardware to download and customise them for their own use.

For example, DeepSeek’s V4-Flash charges US$0.14 per million standard input tokens and US$0.28 per million output tokens. By comparison, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol charges US$4 and US$20, respectively, while Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 costs US$10 and US$50.
DeepSeek accounted for 22.7 per cent of text requests on OpenRouter as of Thursday, the largest share of any model developer, ahead of Google’s 20.4 per cent and OpenAI’s 19.6 per cent, according to the platform’s live rankings.
However, cost is not the only hurdle facing widespread agent adoption.
Agents could generate code, analysis and documents faster than employees could vet them, potentially shifting the operational bottleneck from AI processing speed to human oversight, according to research from the MIT Sloan School of Management published in June.

data.title: Hong Kong mega bridge’s popularity squeezes helicopter, ferry services: lawmaker
data.description:
The number of vehicles using a mega bridge linking Hong Kong with Zhuhai and Macau hit a record high last year, the South China Morning Post has learned, with a lawmaker saying the boom has taken a heavy toll on ferry services and a long-running helicopter service.
Transport Department figures obtained by the SCMP showed that vehicle flow via the popular Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge reached a record high of 5.21 million last year, up more than 19 per cent from 4.36 million in 2024.
The 2025 figures were the highest in the past five years, following border closures due to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021. The bridge was opened for traffic in 2018.
The average daily vehicle flow via the bridge in June this year reached 15,408, already surpassing last year’s figure.
The bridge’s peak in popularity coincided with helicopter service operator Sky Shuttle announcing last week that it would axe its scheduled flights between Hong Kong and Macau, which had operated since 1990.
Sky Shuttle said the service suspension took into account the coming relocation of Macau Heliport to the new heliport at Macau International Airport Terminal 2. It added that its Macau-Shenzhen route was excluded from this suspension and would operate as a scheduled flight service.
Starting this month, the company said its helicopter services would switch to a charter-only model, operating five days a week.
The Sky Shuttle network, which links Macau’s Outer Harbour Ferry Terminal with Hong Kong’s Hong Kong–Macau Ferry Terminal, used to offer 54 flights every day since 2008 with fares set at HK$4,580 (US$584) per trip.
The service was initially founded in 1988 as a joint venture that was majority-owned by Sociedade de Turismo e Diversoes de Macau, headed by the late Macau casino tycoon Stanley Ho.

Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said he believed the bridge’s greater advantages, shown by its boom, had greatly affected the Sky Shuttle business. It also took a toll on Hong Kong-Macau ferry services which recorded a 6.5 per cent year-on-year drop to 7.74 million passengers in 2025.
“The bridge’s greater popularity showed that more commuters were attracted by its advantages over other transport means such as the Sky Shuttle and the Hong Kong-Macau ferry services,” he said.
Chong pointed out that Sky Shuttle’s helicopter services were more expensive and prone to weather disruptions, while ferry services were restricted by their schedules.
“If you commute via the bridge, you can still arrange a luxury service such as pickup or ride services by a limousine,” he said.
Macau government data show 1,112 tourists arrived in Macau via the Outer Harbour heliport in the first seven months of 2026, up 1.7 per cent from a year earlier but down 84.4 per cent from 7,121 in the same period in 2019, before the pandemic. Macau received 24.49 million visitors over the first seven months of 2026.
Annual helicopter arrivals peaked in 2013 at 43,218, during the casino city’s gaming boom, according to the Macau government.
